stories.headline: Andhra Pradesh Minister tells official to expedite restoration works in cyclone-hit towns
stories.title: Andhra Pradesh Minister tells official to expedite restoration works in cyclone-hit towns
stories.summary: Of the 85 locations in 10 municipalities affected by Cyclone Arnab, normalcy has been restored in 71 locations across seven municipalities so far, say officials
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Municipal Administration and Urban Development Minister P. Narayana on Thursday directed the officials to expedite restoration works and bring life back to normal in cyclone-affected areas across Andhra Pradesh.

During a teleconference with Municipal Administration Department Commissioner and Director P. Sampath Kumar, Public Health Engineering-in-Chief Prabhakar and Municipal Commissioners, the Minister reviewed the damage caused by Cyclone Arnab and the progress of relief and restoration measures.
Officials informed the Minister that 85 locations in 10 municipalities across eight districts had been affected by the cyclone.
Normalcy had been restored in 71 locations across seven municipalities so far, they said.
The officials said that fallen trees and electric poles had been cleared.
In areas where power supply remained disrupted, drinking water was being supplied using generators to ensure that residents did not face shortages.
Mr. Narayana instructed the Municipal Commissioners to prioritise sanitation and maintain cleanliness in affected localities to prevent public health problems.
He directed officials to ensure that streetlights were fully functional by Thursday evening.
The Minister stressed the need for coordinated efforts among departments to complete the restoration works swiftly.

stories.headline: Post-Arnab cyclone, heavy rain wreaks havoc in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati districts
stories.title: Post-Arnab cyclone, heavy rain wreaks havoc in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati districts
stories.summary: More than 200 villages in 22 blocks across Ganjam and Gajapati districts severely affected; roads washed away, villages marooned and three rivers are in spate
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Heavy rain triggered by cyclone Arnab wreaked havoc in Odisha’s Ganjam, Gajapati and Kandhamal districts on Thursday (October 29, 2026), washing away roads, marooning villages and triggering landslides, as State officials struggled to restore normalcy.
The rainfall recorded in the three districts was among the highest ever recorded.
“Exceptionally heavy rainfall occurred over south Odisha during the past 24 hours, ending at 8.30 a.m. on Thursday.

The highest rainfall of 546 mm was recorded at Patrapur [Ganjam], followed by 503 mm at Sorada [Ganjam], 462 mm at G. Udayagiri [Kandhamal], 458 mm at Mahendragarh [Gajapati], 388 mm at Sanakhemundi [Ganjam] and 309 mm at Chikiti (Ganjam),” the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
A stretch of the National Highway 326 connecting Berhampur with Mohana was washed away by swirling floodwaters, disrupting road connectivity.
Road infrastructure also suffered extensive damage in Gajapati district.
The hilly terrain compounded the situation, as torrents of rainwater rushed downhill into low-lying areas, triggering landslides and damaging infrastructure.
At several places, floodwaters flowed over major roads, halting vehicular movement in the two districts.
In Ganjam district alone, 42,500 people were marooned by floodwaters, while 11,000 people were shifted from vulnerable areas to designated shelters.
With roads cut off and hundreds of villages inundated by floodwaters in Ganjam, the State government roped in the Coast Guard to airlift people stranded in Dharakote block.

“In response to a distress call received from the Ganjam district administration on the morning of October 29, 2026, the Coast Guard Air Enclave, Bhubaneswar, scrambled an ALH Mk-III helicopter despite severe weather conditions,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.
“Despite challenging conditions, the aircrew located the heavily inundated Public Health Centre in Jagmohan, where people were stranded by floodwaters following the storm.

stories.headline: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan; Assam, Bengal districts on flood alert
stories.title: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan; Assam, Bengal districts on flood alert
stories.summary: Glacial lake outburst in Bhutan; Assam, Bengal districts on flood alert
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A reported glacial lake outburst in Bhutan prompted evacuation warnings downstream in West Bengal.
Authorities are assessing the discharge while monitoring the Sankosh River for a possible surge.
A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) has been reported at Shintaphu Lake in Bhutan, raising concerns over a sudden surge of water flowing downstream into India.
The Government of India has issued a special advisory for parts of West Bengal and Assam, warning that water levels could rise sharply along the Sankosh River.
The outburst was reported on Thursday evening at Shintaphu Lake, located below Wakila Mountain in Lungo, Laya Gewog, in Bhutan's Gasa district.
Sirens were sounded to alert people living near riverbanks, while residents in the affected area were reportedly moved to safer ground.
Shintaphu Lake is among Bhutan's 17 potentially dangerous glacial lakes.

An official from the National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology (NCHM) said a water-level monitoring station was located at Taktsimakhang, but no alert had been triggered there at the time of the initial reports.
The extent of the outburst and its downstream impact remained unclear.
A GLOF occurs when water stored in a lake formed by melting glaciers is suddenly released, often after a natural barrier fails or is breached.
The resulting surge can travel rapidly through mountain valleys, carrying debris and damaging settlements, roads, bridges and farmland.
Shintaphu Lake lies within Bhutan's Punatsangchhu river basin.

stories.headline: Supreme Court strikes down Karnataka law validating ‘corrupt’ 2011 recruitment
stories.title: Supreme Court strikes down Karnataka law validating ‘corrupt’ 2011 recruitment
stories.summary: Top court says cancellation of the recruitment process was upheld by both HC and SC, and that the 'power does not lie with the legislature to annul the cancellation, even by a legislation, and thus nullify the judgments of the Constitutional courts’
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'strikes down' in title weight 40
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 29, 2026) declared unconstitutional a Karnataka State law, which validated the 2011 selection of Gazetted Probationers made through what the court described as a “corrupt” and “blatantly nepotistic” recruitment process conducted by the State Public Service Commission.

A Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran held that the Karnataka Civil Services (Validation of Selection and Appointment of 2011 Batch Gazetted Probationers) Act, 2022, was enacted clearly with the intent to countermand the judgments of both the Karnataka High Court and the Supreme Court.
The courts had upheld the decision to cancel the entire 2011 recruitment process for 362 posts of Group ‘A’ and ‘B’ Officers.

“The cancellation having been upheld by the High Court and the Supreme Court, the power does not lie with the legislature to annul the cancellation, even by a legislation, and thus nullify the judgments of the Constitutional courts,” Justice Chandran said.
The court highlighted how the State government, represented by senior advocate Kapil Sibal, constantly changed its position over a decade “depending on the hues and colours in the changing times”.

The State had, over the years, swung between supporting the cancellation of the entire recruitment process and enacting the 2022 law, leaving the hapless candidates caught in the crosshairs of shifting political whims and systemic failure.

“When the winds of politics change direction, it is the common man who gets caught in the storm… A recruitment of 2011 is hanging fire still, putting to peril the aspirations of many… Six appellants [represented by senior advocate Shyam Divan] who would be over-aged now have relentlessly pursued their cause in their zeal to join the Karnataka Civil Services,” Justice Chandran observed.
The 2011 recruitment process saw 1,38,307 people apply.

Two years later, a Criminal Investigation Department (CID) inquiry found “gross manipulations” in the process, and “the irregularities in evaluation of answer scripts were found to be shockingly disgraceful”.
On Thursday, the Supreme Court upheld the cancellation of the entire recruitment based on a 2011 notification.
It said no equity could be granted to untainted successful candidates, represented by senior advocate Sanjay Nuli, who were selected on the strength of the 2022 Act.
The court termed the Act a “stillborn legislation”.

stories.headline: Our orders breached ‘left and right’, Deepavali was a festival of lights before gunpowder, Supreme Court says in firecrackers case
stories.title: Our orders breached ‘left and right’, Deepavali was a festival of lights before gunpowder, Supreme Court says in firecrackers case
stories.summary: A complete ban may have a ‘spiralling effect’, the court says, asks the Centre and the Delhi government to ensure enforcement against sellers of spurious and banned crackers
reasons: source: event has 2 copies, primary source counted once
corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 29, 2026) said its orders, year after year, to curb and even ban firecrackers during Deepavali, had been violated “left and right”.
A Bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale said the right to religious freedom was also subject to public health and the protection of fundamental rights.

Justice Sundresh said the incessant bursting of firecrackers takes a toll on the health of a large section of the population, including children, the aged, the sick, pregnant women, and specially-abled persons.
Justice Sundresh reminded that Deepavali is called the ‘festival of lights’.
“The problem might have started with gun powder,” the judge said.
The court was hearing a case on the increase in pollution as the festival drew near amidst the loud bangs of firecrackers.
“We understand the sentiments of the public.
If we think in a logical sense, celebrations do boost morale,” Justice Sundresh said.
The court also empathised with officers’ hesitations to book criminal cases against ordinary people who were “enthusiastic” about celebrations.
Justice Sundresh said the court was not in favour of a complete ban.
“That may have a spiralling effect.
But having said that, please do not push us to take harsh actions,” the Bench said.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court Collegium has approved the proposal for appointment of nine advocates as Judges of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.
The decision was taken at a Collegium meeting held on October 29, 2026, according to a statement issued by the Supreme Court Collegium.
The recommendations follow an earlier exercise by the High Court Collegium, headed by Chief Justice Arun Palli, which had recommended 11 names for appointment as High Court Judges in April this year.
The recommendations comprised 10 advocates from the Bar quota and one judicial officer from the Bench quota.
The earlier recommendations were part of an exercise to address vacancies in the High Court, whose sanctioned strength had been increased from 17 to 25 Judges in November 2024.

stories.headline: Scenario of Livestock and Agriculture in Pre and Post- Independent India: Introspection
stories.title: Scenario of Livestock and Agriculture in Pre and Post- Independent India: Introspection
stories.summary: Livestock and agriculture production is considered as the backbone of India’s economy and food security. Despite rapid industrialization, over 46% of India’s total workforce is engaged in agriculture and allied sectors, while roughly 60-65% of the population depends on it for their primary livelihood. However, these sectors have undergone an intense transformation since independence of India in 1947. Indian agriculture during pre- independence was characterized by traditional farming practices like using of tillers, sickles and manual labour with little or no mechanization which eventually resulted in low productivity. Livestock has traditionally complemented crop cultivation by providing a source of draught power, manure, milk and hence an additional household income. It also provided financial security to the families during periods of economic distress. Immediately after independence, India faced widespread poverty, low agricultural productivity and an urgent need to strengthen India’s economy. Following independence, agricultural research, irrigation facilities, improved seeds, fertilization and mechanization gradually transformed agricultural and livestock production. Over time, these initiatives contributed to major agricultural transformations commonly described as Green, White, Blue and Golden Revolutions. The history of livestock and agricultural development cannot be understood only through the increase in production. An introspective assessment must also examine who benefited from these developments, what environmental burdens accompanied them and whether leads to lasting prosperity for farmers and other livestock owners. Cattle and buffaloes served draught power while manure was used as a fertilizer for soil. Milk and its byproducts served as a household nutrition and also provided income. Indigenous breeds had valuable adaptive characteristics like tolerance to local climatic conditions and ability to survive under low input management systems. But, livestock productivity was restricted by insufficient nutrition, infectious diseases and parasitic infections. Treatment of animals in many rural areas depended on traditional knowledge and locally available traditional remedies and access to veterinary hospitals was limited. Dairy marketing was also unorganized and inadequate milk collection, chilling, processing and transportation facilities limited the commercial potential of livestock production. Limited availability of scientific support and organized infrastructure further restricted their capacity to improve production. Farming was primarily meeting the household food requirements and there was a limited access to modern agricultural machinery, irrigation and other scientific facilities. Due to inadequate irrigation, limited availability of good quality seeds and insufficient fertilizers, agricultural productivity was also low. Farmers were prone to droughts, floods and other natural calamities. Poor storage and transportation facilities further restricted the movement of agricultural production and increased post-harvest losses. Colonial land revenue system further contributed to unequal relationships between land-owners and cultivators. This practice often limited farmers’ ability to invest in irrigation, soil improvement and other long-term agricultural assets which ultimately lead to crop failure, disease outbreaks and other economic losses. Before the widespread expansion of monetized rural markets, barter and customary exchange arrangements played important roles in various village economies. Livestock and agricultural produce was exchanged for essential items and household goods. Sometimes, occupational groups used to receive a share of the produce and harvest in return for their services. These arrangements strengthened interdependence within rural communities but it also restricted economic exchange only to local networks and limit farmers’ bargaining power and accumulate savings. As commercial agriculture expanded, monetary transactions and regulated markets gradually became more important. Farmers gained more opportunities to sell their produce for money and purchase essential inputs like seeds, fertilizers, machinery etc. But this transition didn’t ensure fair returns to primary producers due to transportation cost, price fluctuation and inadequate storage. The historical transition from barter to organized agricultural marketing indicates an important economic change but it also reflects the need for transparent markets and profitable prices. The abolition of intermediary landholding systems, tenancy reforms and redistribution of surplus land were intended to minimize exploitation and the condition of cultivators. However, its application varied from state to state. Incomplete land records, resistance from powerful landowners meant that landlessness and unequal access to productive resources persisted. Land fragmentation was the other major challenge. Population growth and subsequent division of agricultural holdings among generations contributed to smaller and more scattered landholdings. These conditions limited the use of machinery, irrigation investments, crop diversification and the economic viability of farming. However, these gains were geographically uneven with irrigated regions generally benefitting more than rain fed areas. The environmental exploitation also became evident with intensive cultivation and excessive groundwater extraction. The extensive usage of fertilizers and pesticides further contributed to the soil degradation, water pollution and ecological disturbances. Operation Flood was implemented in phases and helped strengthen India’s dairy infrastructure, organised milk procurement and rural dairy economy. Inadequate green fodder, high feed costs, reproductive disorders, mastitis and heat stress decreased the productivity and hence profitability. Moreover indiscriminate crossbreeding without taking attention to nutrition and healthcare compromised animal welfare. However, the expansion of fisheries created environmental concerns like water pollution, eutrophication, habitat destruction, disease outbreaks in intensive aquaculture and salanisation of agricultural land. Rural roads and the expansion of agricultural markets improved connectivity between producers and consumers. Timely diagnosis of diseases, access to qualified veterinary professionals and responsible use of medicines remain essential for sustainable livestock development. In livestock sector also, the benefits didn’t reach all livestock owners equally and there was also shortage of veterinary services, inadequate fodder and insufficient infrastructure. Poor manure management can contribute to water contamination and inadequate waste disposal and unsuitable housing can affect animal health. Climate change presents an additional challenge to livestock production by affecting temperature patterns, rainfall distribution, water availability, fodder production and the condition of grazing and pasture lands. Livestock may consequently face changing risks from emerging, re-emerging and endemic infectious diseases. Changes in disease ecology can also complicate surveillance and control, while the evolution and spread of pathogens may increase the challenges faced by veterinary health systems. The following priorities deserve attention: Sustainable crop production by promoting soil testing, balanced fertilisation, improved seed quality and climate resilient farming practices. Efficient water management by encouraging rainwater harvesting, groundwater monitoring and cropping patterns compatible with local water availability. Improved market infrastructure by strengthening rural roads, storage and processing facilities and transparent marketing. Affordable veterinary healthcare by expanding veterinary services, timely disease diagnosis and access to qualified veterinary professionals. Integrated livestock management by improving fodder availability, balanced rations, reproductive management, hygienic milk production and prevention of economically important diseases. Responsible breeding programmes by combining improved genes with adaptability, fertility, disease resistance and animal welfare. Environmental protection by reducing pollution, encouraging manure management and efficient and judicious use of chemical fertilisers, pesticides, veterinary drugs and water resources. Traditional farming system based on animal power, local resources and barter system has been supplemented by scientific crop production, mechanisation, organised markets, and improved livestock breeding and modern veterinary healthcare. The Green Revolution strengthened food security, White Revolution transformed dairy sector, Blue Revolution improved fisheries sector and Golden Revolution increased the horticulture production. However, increased production has not eliminated land fragmentation, livestock related financial pressures or environmental degradation. Farmers continue to face challenges with fluctuating prices, natural calamities and limited infrastructure. The future of Indian livestock and agriculture industry depends on balancing productivity with profitability, environmental responsibility, economic security of farmers and long-term resilience of rural communities. ( The Author is HOD Veterinary Medicine, SKUAST Kashmir)
